title: Every word scores the final arrow
allegory: The unembedding is a line of judges, one per word in the vocabulary, each holding their own arrow; they score the model's final arrow by how far it points along theirs, and those scores are the logits.
map: the residual vector at a position, after the final LayerNorm
one judge per word, holding their own arrow
one column of W_U per vocabulary token
a judge's score: how far your arrow points along theirs
logit = residual · W_U[:, token] (plus the bias b_U)
turning all the scores into odds
softmax over the logits, done later by the loss or the sampler
judges don't care where an arrow came from
linearity: any piece of the residual stream can be unembedded (logit lens, DLA)
credit: The picture of a final matrix that scores every word, followed by softmax turning scores into odds, follows 3Blue1Brown's 'But what is a GPT?' (Deep Learning series).

chapters.name: The last step
chapters.note: a list of numbers in, a score per word out?

cap.1: At the end of the model sits one long list of numbers: its final thought. But you need a score for every word it might say next. How?
cap.2: The residual stream ends as one d_model-sized vector per position. What you need is a score (a logit) for each of the d_vocab tokens. One matrix does the conversion.
cap.3: The final residual (after ln_final) must be mapped to d_vocab logits. The unembedding W_U, shape (d_model, d_vocab), is that linear readout.

cap.1: Line up one judge for every word in the dictionary. Each holds their own arrow and scores the model's final arrow by how well it points along theirs.
cap.2: W_U has one column per token. A token's logit is the dot product of the final residual with that token's column: big when they point the same way.
cap.3: logits = x·W_U + b_U with x the post-ln_final residual. Column W_U[:, t] is token t's readout direction; the logit is a projection onto it, scaled by its norm.

cap.1: Each score is one multiply-and-add: pair up the two arrows' numbers, multiply each pair, add it all up. Same direction: big score. Opposite: very negative.
cap.2: All words at once is one matrix multiply: x @ W_U + b_U gives a logit per token. The Unembed exercise is this multiply plus a bias.
cap.3: An einsum over d_model: (batch, pos, d_model) × (d_model, d_vocab) → (batch, pos, d_vocab), plus b_U. Softmax comes later, inside the loss or the sampler.

chapters.name: A tiny dictionary
chapters.title: toy W_U: one column per word; final arrow x = [2, 1, 0]

cap.1: A tiny model: arrows of 3 numbers, a 4-word dictionary. Each column is one word's arrow. With final arrow [2, 1, 0], dog scores 2 + 1 + 0 = 3 and wins.
cap.2: x @ W_U: cat = 2·1 + 1·0 + 0·1 = 2, dog = 3, sat = 1, the = 0. Real GPT-2 is the same picture with far more rows and columns.
cap.3: Each logit is a column-wise inner product. Rows are residual dimensions, so reading a row of W_U shows how one dimension votes across the whole vocabulary.

cap.1: The judges don't care where an arrow came from. Hold up a half-finished thought, or one part's contribution, and they still tell you which words it favours.
cap.2: Unembedding is linear, so you can apply W_U to anything in the residual stream: a middle layer (the logit lens), one head's output (direct logit attribution), a steering vector.
cap.3: Logits decompose over residual summands. The logit lens applies ln_final and W_U mid-model; DLA projects each component's output; unembedding a steering vector reveals its top tokens.

chapters.name: Logits, not probabilities
chapters.verdict: Measure in logits; softmax only at the very end.

cap.1: Scores add up nicely; odds don't. Once scores become odds, each word's odds depend on every other word, so the parts stop adding up.
cap.2: Logit difference, logit[' Mary'] − logit[' John'], is one dot product with W_U[:, Mary] − W_U[:, John], so contributions add. Probabilities pass through softmax and don't.
cap.3: Softmax is nonlinear, so log-probs don't decompose over components; logit differences do. Caveat: ln_final divides everything by a prompt-dependent scale before W_U.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Logit lens: read the middle of the model
Unembed a steering vector to see what it says

cap.1: This one matrix is your window into the model: hold any internal arrow up to the word judges and see what it is trying to say.
cap.2: You will reuse W_U constantly: logit lens, direct logit attribution, OV circuits, and sanity-checking a steering vector by unembedding it. It is the model's own dictionary.
cap.3: W_U is the fixed readout basis that makes internal directions legible: logit lens, DLA and full OV circuits (W_U W_OV W_E) all use it to understand and steer model behaviour.

coda.title: Aim the final arrow at four word judges and read the odds

caption.1: Slide the arrow's tip around and watch which word wins. Then raise the length: same winner, far more sure. Direction picks the word; length sets the confidence.
caption.2: Bars are softmax of x·W_U for four toy word columns. Paris and France point close together, so they rise and fall together. Scaling x keeps the ranking but sharpens the odds.
caption.3: Logit = |x||w|cos θ per token, so scaling x by c is softmax at temperature 1/c. The logit-difference readout stays exactly linear in x even as the probabilities saturate.

where_else: Logit lens: unembed the middle of the model to watch its guess form
Direct logit attribution: unembed each head's output to see what it pushes
OV circuits: W_U W_OV W_E, what a head writes about a token it attends to
Any classifier's final linear layer: one score per class, then softmax

hamming.what: The final matrix that scores every vocabulary token by a dot product with the last residual vector, producing the logits.
hamming.when: At the end of every forward pass, and any time you want to read what an internal vector says in words.
hamming.why: Because it is linear, any piece of the residual stream can be read through it, which makes it the main window interpretability uses to see what a model is doing.

object.title: The word tent
object.subtitle: The ground is every possible final arrow; the height is the best score any word gives it, and each flat facet belongs to one word.

cap.1: Every point on the ground is a possible final arrow. The height is the best score any word gives it. Each flat facet belongs to one word.
cap.2: Surface height = max over tokens of x·W_U[:, t] for a 2-D toy residual x.
cap.3: The max of linear functions is convex and piecewise linear; each facet is the region where one token has the top logit.

cap.1: From above, the ground is carved into territories. Wherever the arrow's tip lands, that territory's word wins.
cap.2: Argmax regions: which token the model would pick greedily for each residual direction.
cap.3: The decision regions of a linear readout are convex cones through the origin, bounded where two logits tie.

cap.1: The ridges are ties. On a ridge two words score the same, and the model is torn between them.
cap.2: Paris and France point close together, so their ridge is gentle: arrows near it give both high scores.
cap.3: Along a ridge x·(W_U[:, a] − W_U[:, b]) = 0: the logit-difference direction is the normal to that boundary.

cap.1: Lengthen the ' the' column and its territory grows: a longer judge's arrow scores higher for arrows pointing its way.
cap.2: Column norm matters as well as direction: a longer W_U column gives bigger logits and wins more of the space.
cap.3: Logits scale with ‖W_U[:, t]‖, so norm acts like a per-token gain on top of direction, shifting the argmax boundaries.

cap.1: Every facet is perfectly flat because scoring is straight-line: double the arrow and every score doubles. The logit lens relies on that.
cap.2: Linearity: unembedding a sum is the sum of unembeddings, which is why you can read one head or one layer on its own.
cap.3: Flat facets are the linearity of W_U made visible; it is what licenses logit-lens readouts and per-component DLA before softmax.

predict.q: You double the length of the final arrow. What happens to the winning word?
predict.why: Doubling x doubles every logit. The ranking stays the same; softmax just gets sharper.

predict.q: Can you apply W_U to one attention head's output on its own?

options.t: Yes: it shows which words that head pushes
No: only the final residual can be unembedded

predict.why: Unembedding is linear, so any piece of the residual stream can be read this way. That is direct logit attribution.

predict.q: Which of these is a single fixed direction in the residual stream?
predict.why: The logit difference is a dot product with W_U[:, Mary] − W_U[:, John]. Probabilities pass through softmax, which is not linear.

object.where: Any linear readout that scores every class at once: a classifier's last layer, a linear probe, a dot-product search.
